newsitem.title: MEXICO: Plans completed for Clinton Mexico trip.
newsitem.headline: Plans completed for Clinton Mexico trip.

text.p: Finalising plans for President Bill Clinton's visit to Mexico, White House special adviser Thomas McLarty on Monday accented the positive side of U.S.-Mexico relations and played down controversial topics.
Clinton will visit Mexico May 5-7, the first stop on a journey that will also take him to Central America and the Caribbean. The trip will be his first to Latin America since he took office in 1993.

Disputes over drug corruption in Mexico and tough new U.S. immigration laws have recently clouded relations but top-level officials on both sides are anxious to smooth over differences ahead of the presidential visit.
"I do not think it is an overstatement to say that our level of cooperation is at an all-time high," McLarty, Clinton's Special Envoy for the Americas, said.

"...I think what we have is a relationship that is a sustaining one, a sustaining relationship where we can make consistent progress over time and take full advantage of the opportunities before us," he told a news conference.
He said Clinton and his wife Hillary were "genuinely excited about returning to Mexico, where they honeymooned."

"President Clinton's visit to Mexico City, only the second U.S. presidential visit to Mexico City in 30 years, will acknowledge, illustrate and underscore the commitment to strengthening our important bilateral relationship," he added.

Underlining the importance of that relationship, McLarty said some 800,000 U.S. jobs were now linked to trade with Mexico and U.S. exports to Mexico -- as well as Mexican exports to the U.S. -- had reached record highs.
Questions about drugs, immigration and rising anti-U.S. feeling in Mexico were diplomatically side-stepped.

"Immigration laws should make borders work. They should not divide our countries but unite our respective countries as friends," McLarty said, stressing that the United States valued the contribution of Hispanic immigrants.

He said Clinton would meet leaders of opposition parties during his visit and denied that the trip amounted to a gesture of support for President Ernesto Zedillo and his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) ahead of key congressional elections in July.
"Obviously in this trip we are not going in any way to interfere with the political election process in any sovereign country," he said. "... We certainly are not going to take any kind of position."
The PRI has ruled Mexico for 68 unbroken years but Zedillo and his predecessor Carlos Salinas have promoted reforms to give opposition parties a greater chance of winning power.

McLarty praised that process, saying: "I believe a third of the offices are held by parties other than the PRI here in Mexico and the last several elections ... have been regarded, I think, as very fair and very open elections."
He added: "That is an affirmation that the seeds of democracy are growing and growing quite well."
